49710903.article_content:
Tell the speakers that you liked their talks
Published by
Ana Rodrigues
on the
14th September 2026
I spent a great chunk of last week at
SmashingConf Freiburg
and it was lovely as usual. It was great to meet some people I've only ever seen online and see old friends. And I am not going to lie - it was pretty flattering to have people come over to me and challenge me to admit I was the mystery speaker (SmashingConf always has a mystery speaker they only announce on the day). I wasn't, as you all know now, but thank you for thinking I am of that calibre!
Anyway, at the after-party I was chatting to a fun group of people and one of them mentioned how someone else in the group really wanted to ask something to one of the speakers from this year but they were feeling shy and intimidated. I immediately encouraged the situation to happen (and it did)! It helps that I am a little bit shameless after a couple of drinks but facilitating speaker and attendee conversations is something I've been trying really hard to make happen whenever I can. So I brought the speaker in question and a few people to join our group pac-man style and people got to chatting.
This reminded me of
when I MCed CSS Day
earlier in June. I tried really hard to encourage people to come and chat with the speakers throughout the event. At the speakers' dinner, I asked every single person I was going to present on stage if it was okay if I did so. Of course they said yes - they are all a wonderful bunch of folks.
But this also comes from my experience as a speaker. I arrived at what people call the "speaker circuit" quite recently and I never experienced the wave of feedback that I know speakers used to experience on Twitter before Twitter was ruined. I know it is super intimidating to approach someone who has just been on a stage as you may think you have nothing to add to the conversation. I've been on that side and I still am on that side too. Trust me - even as a speaker or MC I am in awe of many people I met this year and I was so afraid of approaching them and chatting to them only for them to realise I am... just a very simple woman.
I've had events I spoke at that I didn't have a single piece of feedback online which made me wonder how flat it landed. It isn't necessarily an ego thing - but sometimes you wonder if you did okay, if people hated it, etc. I'm only human, gang. But I know I am not the only speaker who has been a bit rattled by silence. I've had a few conversations with other speakers about what to do when there isn't a lot of feedback on a talk. It was good to chat this through as I thought it was a me problem but turns out, after all, no thought is original.
And I need to be better at this myself. Most times, I forget to compliment my own friends who are speaking because, bizarrely, I assume they can read my mind and know that I love their work and I am on the first row cheering them on. I need to live-post more and I need to blog more because I really want people to see the amazing conferences I attend, with fantastic organisers and incredible speakers.
These days, especially if I have an active role in an event, I feel a little bit shy and probably stick around close to people I know more than I should. After I speak on a stage, my brain is rambling on about all the things I know I said incorrectly and all the details I know weren't perfect.
So, if you always wanted to but think it isn't worth telling a speaker you liked their talk, this is your encouragement post to do so. It is always worth it even if it is a small tap and small chat. People put a lot of work into it and they want people to enjoy it and, at least for me, I kinda do want to know if we did alright.

data.title: Original Sony PlayStation 2 security chip 'broken wide open' after 26 years
data.author: rbanffy
data.article_summary: 加拿大复古硬件爱好者DiscoStarslayer历经四年，成功逆向工程并提取初代“厚机”PS2中的CXP102064 MechaCon芯片固件。该芯片负责光驱控制及游戏、记忆卡安全验证。成果将助力PS2硬件维修、游戏保存、模拟器和自制软件开发，并可能推动光驱替代方案，还惠及部分街机系统。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：PS2 MechaCon（尤其SPC970）被破解/倾倒后的技术意义、实际用途及游戏保存价值。

不同观点：
• 逆向工程团队称：目前已可通过记忆卡、硬盘或DVD漏洞运行备份；50K及更新型号可用“force unlock”补丁，无需修改盗版光盘。ROM倾倒本身不足以制作硬件ODE，但可能支持替代MechaCon的改装芯片。  
• 这些数据有助于低层模拟器开发，解析MagicGate、KELF/KIRX安全机制，也可用于寻找漏洞，推动MechaPwn、TonyHax等功能（解锁光盘类型、LBN或PS1模式）。但普通游戏光盘内容并未加密，除DNAS认证外，倾倒不会额外解锁游戏。  
• 有人期待其改善游戏保存与模拟器开发，甚至认为可帮助提供合法可用的PS2 BIOS；也有人指出未来主机依赖在线服务和首日补丁，保存难度更大。  
• 技术过程受到赞叹：包括化学开盖、显微镜光学读取，最终因软件漏洞而无需继续进行部分艰苦操作；社区还开发了SPC970的Ghidra反编译器并公开倾倒数据。

补充讨论：争议焦点是“破解是否带来实际新能力”。评论者询问能否制作ODE、破解此前无法MechaPwn的型号及直接用于BIOS；逆向者则强调其主要价值是安全研究、漏洞利用和低层保存，而非立即实现硬件模拟或解密游戏。也有评论认为PS2已发布多年，成果的现实意义有限。

The ‘magic
security
chip’ inside the original
PlayStation 2
has been successfully reverse-engineered and dumped. Canadian retro hardware and software enthusiast DiscoStarslayer was the manic mind behind the cracking open of the CXP102064 MechaCon chip, which arrived inside the ‘PS2 Fat’ from 1999. It took “four years of effort” to reach this stage, but this milestone should be a boon to hardware preservation, repair, and
emulation
projects.
After 4 years of effort, I'm happy to announce that one of the final secrets of the PS2 has been broken wide open!It's been a long process of decapping, optical dumping, and now at last a software solution.Thank you Libby for finding the exploit from our dirty optical dumps! pic.twitter.com/VrsCH8I35C
September 13, 2026
The Mechacon got its name from its primary duty of controlling the PS2’s optical and flash drive mechanics. It also played a significant part in
Sony
’s game optical disc security, supporting “Magic Gate [memory card] and KELF file [executable] decryption among other things,” notes the
PSDev Wiki.
Unlocking the secret workings of such chips can be important to those involved in video game preservation. So, many people will appreciate DiscoStarslayer’s work in
reverse engineering
and dumping one of the PS2’s last remaining secrets.
As per the social media post, the arduous task of breaking the MechaCon’s security took four years. Some of the reverse engineering tricks utilized by DiscoStarslayer include chemically
decapping
the CXP102064 to expose the die, then using microscopes and optical dumping skills to analyze the silicon chip circuitry. In this case, a lucky break during the hacking apparently uncovered an exploit that provided a method whereby the chip’s data could be extracted through software.
Latest Videos From
Tom's Hardware
Watch full video here:
With this achievement unlocked, the game/hardware preservation and programming communities can look forward to improved emulation and homebrew developments. It should also open up possibilities for replacing the aging
optical drives
in PS2 consoles.
Beyond the confines of
PS2
Fat consoles, some social media commenters noted that the MechaCon was also used in a handful of arcade machines from the era. Specifically, the Namco System 246 and System 256, as well as the Konami Python 1, which used modified PS2 hardware, used the MechaCon firmware to authenticate security and allow the execution of encrypted game data.

data.author: 6LLvveMx2koXfwn
data.article_summary: 文章讲述《神秘博士》未完成故事《Shada》的幕后经历。1979年，剧组在剑桥取景，汤姆·贝克饰演的博士拍摄撑船戏时屡次落水。由于BBC罢工，伦敦棚内拍摄被迫中断，剧集长期成为影迷传说。2017年，贝克与演员通过补录台词和动画，终于完成并发布了这个故事。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：围绕《Doctor Who》未完成剧集《Shada》的不同版本、衍生作品及其文化关联展开讨论。

不同观点：
• 有人推荐阅读维基百科，特别指出《Shada》与道格拉斯·亚当斯《Dirk Gently’s Holistic Detective Agency》之间的联系。
• 有人最喜欢原始未完成版本，也赞赏2017年动画版，认为动画补足了原版仅靠旁白留下的叙事空白；并推荐经典《Doctor Who》或亚当斯作品爱好者购买蓝光。
• 有人补充介绍了多个音频版本，包括保罗·麦卡恩主演的版本，以及20世纪80至90年代BBC尝试制作、由汤姆·贝克为缺失片段配旁白并发行VHS的版本。

49689062.article_content:
Image caption,
The Doctor punting in Cambridge with his companion Romana
By
Aimee Dexter
Â
and
Â
Alice Whaley
Published
12 September 2026
For more than six decades, Doctor Who has taken viewers across time and space.
But hidden within the show's history are unfinished episodes recorded in Cambridge.
In 1979, production teams arrived in the university city following a storyline called 'Shada', written by local author Douglas Adams - featuring Tom Baker as the fourth Doctor.
However, not everything went smoothly during the shoot.
Speaking on a new
BBC Sounds documentary Doctor Who: Lost in Cambridge
,  Marcus Hearn said his father, who was a porter at Clare College, saw first-hand some of the challenges the crew and Baker faced while filming.
The Doctor Who Magazine editor said: "Tom Baker had been struggling to learn how to punt and he kept falling into the Cam.
"It was my dad's job to provide him with blankets and brandy, and to basically try to calm him down because apparently he was in a very bad mood."
Image caption,
Tom Baker was filmed punting in Cambridge as part of a series of unfinished Doctor Who episodes
The story finds the Doctor in Cambridge working alongside Romana and a retired Time Lord, Professor Chronotis, to defeat the evil alien Skagra who is attempting to steal the secrets to the prison planet, Shada.
The episodes were filmed for the end of the show's 17th series.
But strike action at the BBC meant studio scenes
were never completed and the episodes were abandoned
.
Hearn said he had "eagerly awaited" the episodes arriving on his television after hearing of his father's adventures.
"I waited and I waited and it just never happened, so it became something of a myth and something of a legend amongst Doctor Who fans from that point onwards."
Image source,
Julie Edwards
Image caption,
Marcus Hearn's father was a porter at a University of Cambridge college during the filming
Author Douglas Adams is best known for writing the famous novel and radio series, The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy.
Born in Cambridge in 1952 and educated in Essex, he returned to Cambridge to study at St John's College.
Talking about Adams, Hearn said: "This was Douglas Adams' world, of course, because he'd been a student at St John's in the early 70s.
"You can still go to St John's and look at his archive, and you could see even when he was a student and before that, he was actually writing Doctor Who stories, even before he was a professional writer."
With 'Shada' being set in and around the University of Cambridge, Hearn added: "Ironically, St John's didn't actually grant the BBC permission to shoot there and so they had to shoot at Emmanuel and Clare instead."
Richard Bignell, author of Doctor Who on Location, said crews also spent time at Grantchester Meadow
"They obviously did a little bit of improvisation as well because when the Doctor first emerges from the TARDIS when it lands, he points out, 'mind that cow pat'," he added.
Image source,
Les McCallum
Image caption,
A designers copy of the film schedule for Shada
Doctor Who: Lost in Cambridge
The tale of the missing Doctor Who storyline filmed in Cambridge.
Listen on Sounds
Les McCallum, a design assistant on Shada, said most of the filming was completed in Cambridge, with the rest planned to be filmed in studios in London.
But, strike action cut the studio filming short, leaving the episodes unfinished.
"We did the recording in the morning and then come lunch time we all went off. We came back and all the studio doors were locked and chained because of the strike," said McCallum.
"We never saw the finished product, and they couldn't get the actors to come back again because they were contracted on other series or other shows, and that's why it never got finished."
Image caption,
Baker returned to complete the story in 2017, 36 years after it was first filmed
In 1983, the show celebrated its 20th anniversary. The producer wanted to reunite all the previous Doctors in a special episode called 'The Five Doctors.' However, Baker declined.
Hearn said: "The BBC very much wanted Tom Baker to be in the show, because it was a big feature-length 20th anniversary TV movie, and then somebody remembered that they had these fragments of this incomplete story in the archive.
"So they went back to the archive, found the bits of Shada, which of course had never been broadcast, and then wrote a story around these fragments and cut them into this TV movie."
36 years after the storyline was abandoned, Baker and the cast finally returned to complete Shada.
Baker and Lalla Ward, who played Romana, recorded the missing lines from Adams' original script, and the visuals were created with animation. This new, partially animated version was released in 2017.

data.title: Show HN: I made a flight simulator, except you're just a passenger
data.author: rkotcher
data.article_summary: 无法获取文章内容
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：围绕一款沉浸式客舱飞行模拟器的真实性、技术表现、实用价值与改进方向展开讨论。

不同观点：
• 赞赏其沉浸感与创意：有人认为能在客舱内走动、从窗口俯瞰城市，真实还原乘客视角；也有人想用它帮助从未乘机者了解飞行，或用于乘客恐飞训练。  
• 强调专业应用价值：飞行模拟工程师介绍，客舱模拟可用于机组撤离训练，通常结合液压平台、多屏视景和主从节点系统。  
• 批评性能优化不足：指出阴影重复渲染、300多个绘制调用、百万级三角形及高分辨率GTAO造成风扇狂转，认为缺少性能分析，属于“氛围驱动但未优化”的作品。另有用户反馈 iPhone 17 Pro 十秒内崩溃。  
• 建议增加功能：希望进度条或座椅屏幕地图可跳转航段，机场可在地图上直接选择，并让航线符合现实空域限制，例如中韩航线应绕行台湾。  
• 以讽刺强化“真实感”：评论者列举婴儿哭闹、占扶手、咳嗽、安检排队、行李故障、糟糕餐食等，将普通航班痛点视为应加入的玩法；也有人建议改做空乘应对乘客冲突的游戏。  
• 有人指出已有类似作品《Airplane Mode》，并质疑客舱细节，如2-2座椅布局却配三盏阅读灯；同时希望项目开源扩展。

补充讨论：争议焦点主要是“趣味创意和沉浸体验”与“技术优化、细节真实性及功能完整度”之间的取舍；部分批评实际以幽默方式表达认可。

data.author: Tomte
data.article_summary: 无法获取文章内容
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：文章《This is how we do modern frequentist statistics》的来源、方法依据，以及统计分析自动化的可能性。

不同观点：
• [wodenokoto] 对文章来源提出质疑：文章被称为现代频率学派统计的介绍，但据称只是《Bayesian Workflows》一书的节选，因此评论者询问文章具体在哪里解释这一点。同时总体认可文章内容，认为文章值得推荐。
• [SubiculumCode] 关注方法细节，询问文中“attractiveness distribution”（吸引力分布）是如何得到的，以及是否来源于相关论文。其核心疑问是数据或分布设定的出处与依据。
• [j7ake] 认为这类统计分析如今应当可以自动完成，理由是编程代理已经非常普及，暗示统计建模、计算和分析流程可以更多交给自动化工具。

补充讨论：评论之间没有直接回应，主要分别聚焦于文章定位、具体统计依据和分析自动化。争议焦点在于：文章是否清楚交代了其理论或数据来源，以及统计工作应由研究者解释和验证，还是可以依赖编程代理自动执行。

data.article_summary: 文章讨论LLM时代学习编程与建立能力的关系。作者认为，AI能快速帮助缺乏基础的人构建复杂系统，却可能造成“会用但不理解”，一旦出错便难以维护和掌控。因此，编程基础、调试、架构及系统性理解仍不可替代。同时，作者担忧AI可能导致程序员及其他知识工作者失业，并对“技术进步必然创造更多工作”的乐观论断持怀疑态度。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：LLM降低了编程实践门槛，却可能让学习者失去理解、调试和维护代码的能力；核心问题是如何在使用AI与掌握编程基础之间取得平衡。

不同观点：
• **AI加速但可能超越理解**：LLM能快速生成复杂MVP，开发速度可能超过个人知识增长；因此必须边做项目边主动补足原理和架构理解（japhyr）。
• **编程基础仍不可替代**：程序最终需要用形式逻辑维护，自然语言提示不能替代对代码的理解；不会编程就无法判断AI输出是否可靠，也难以独立修复问题（js8、agentultra）。
• **AI是双刃剑**：专家可借此提效，但依赖AI会削弱能力；初学者可能做出“看起来能用”的作品，却陷入不会推理、调试和维护的循环（duendefm、bborud）。
• **支持“边做边学”**：AI可以生成真实项目、解释代码、协助调试，形成个性化课程；关键在于保持好奇，而不是只要求“能运行”（dack、RugnirViking）。
• **提倡受控协作**：保留手写项目，先理解数据结构、算法和架构，再让AI实现、审查或提出方案，以维持人的判断力和代码质量（aethertap、ah1508）。
• **学习编程本身仍有价值**：编程不仅是就业技能，也带来乐趣、创造力和解决问题的能力；手写和阅读文档者可能拥有更强的长期优势（utopiah、threepts、lolakutty）。

补充讨论：争议焦点在于AI究竟会扩大编程普及、创造新岗位，还是造成技能退化与过度依赖；关于中国加入WTO的类比，评论者认为就业会转移和重组，但不能简单证明AI不会造成失业。

49723873.article_content:
On learning programming in an age of LLMs
by Mark Seemann
Open answers to a reader's letter.
A reader recently wrote me a long letter with lots of questions about learning programming in this age of LLMs. After a bit of back-and-forth, I got permission to quote extensively from the letter in order to attempt some answers in public.
None of my answers I consider particularly rigorous; the situation is so uncertain that I can only answer to the best of my abilities, but I don't claim them to hold any kind of immutable truth.
"I'm trying to understand how people who deeply understand software think about learning and competence in the age of AI. I'm approaching it almost as a historian would: asking people directly how they make sense of a technological transition while actually living through it.
"About a year ago I became fascinated by AI-assisted programming. Despite having no formal CS background, with LLMs I managed to build a fairly large TypeScript/JavaScript system involving APIs, PostgreSQL, LLM pipelines, research automation and multi-model workflows. At first it felt almost magical: AI seemed to collapse the distance between having an idea and being able to build it.
"But now I'm trying to turn that system into a real production product, and I'm struggling. I fix one error with AI, then another appears, then another part behaves in a way I don't fully understand. After months of refactoring I had an uncomfortable realization: I may have built a system that is above my own level of understanding. When everything works, that gap is almost invisible. When it doesn't, it becomes very real.
"Sometimes I genuinely don't know what to do next without asking another model. That made me wonder whether I spent a year building a product, or partly building the appearance of one: something sophisticated enough to work, but which I don't yet understand deeply enough to truly own.
"I'm not anti-AI at all. I'm fascinated by these systems and want to work with them professionally. But I'm unsure what the right relationship with them should be."
Indeed, I'm not sure either, but before proceeding, I find it most transparent to reveal my position. I haven't yet decided on AI, but
I lean toward disliking it
, knowing full well that it may be unstoppable.
I do work and experiment with it, and it often impresses me. At other times, it frustrates me. It's usually when it impresses me the most that I resent it maximally.
When it's bad, it can be frustrating, but then at least I can absorb an ember of warmth in the illusion that what I've spent more than thirty years learning is still relevant. When it's at its best, I sometimes think:
Where do I sign up for
the Butlerian jihad
?
My position on LLMs is only partly based on my own socio-economic status. I'm old enough, and have had enough success already, that all other things being equal, I can survive unemployment. I'm not sure, on the other hand, than any knowledge-based society can.
It may be that LLMs will take programmer jobs before they take other white-collar jobs. After all, programming
may
be a discipline where verification is easier than, say, insurance claims management. Still, if we reach a point of mass unemployment among knowledge workers, I'm not sure society as we know it will survive.
I usually don't talk much about my background as an economist, but in this context I find it relevant to mention. As an economist, I can't imagine that mass unemployment of 30-40% will not have a significant impact on the economy.
I'm painfully aware of the arguments that this has happened before: There may be job loss, but the advance of technology leads to new jobs we can't even imagine today. It was like that with the introduction of the
stocking frame
, the steam engine, the internal combustion engine, computers, etc. This is only partly true: Yes, new jobs were created, but often not for those people who lost their jobs. Coal miners didn't just become programmers overnight.
The same kind of argument was used when
China was admitted to the World Trade Organization
. And indeed, lots of new jobs were created, just not in the Western world.
So, based on lived and historical experience, I'm sceptical of arguments that all will be fine.
But I sincerely hope that I'm wrong. I love to program, and wouldn't mind doing it for another ten years. Perhaps more importantly, I have young adult children. I hope that there's a world for them, too.
"So I'd really like to know how you think about this. Are you glad you learned programming fundamentals before LLMs existed? If you were starting today, would you still seriously study languages, data structures, databases, networking, operating systems, debugging and architecture? Do you think AI can let people become capable of building much faster than they become capable of understanding?"
Am I glad that I learned programming before LLMs? Yes, of course. Those skills served me well for thirty years.

data.title: Intelligence per Watt: Measuring Intelligence Efficiency of Local AI
data.author: pythonic_hell
data.article_summary: 文章提出“每瓦智能度”（IPW）指标，用单位能耗衡量本地语言模型的任务准确率。研究评估了20多个模型、8种硬件及100万条真实查询，发现本地模型可处理88.7%的问题。2023—2025年，IPW提升5.3倍，可本地处理的查询比例从23.2%增至71.3%。但本地加速器效率仍比云端低至少1.4倍，优化空间显著。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：论文以“单位功耗的任务能力（IPW）”比较本地与云端大模型，引发对指标有效性、能耗测量和实际部署价值的讨论。

不同观点：
• 支持本地部署：本地模型响应更快、行为稳定、可避免数据收集与转售，GPU冬季还能兼作室内加热；合规场景下，“质量/瓦”直接关系预算。有人以 Ollama、Neo4j 和 Qwen2.5:3B 为例，称本地完成简单 NL-to-Cypher 仅需3–5秒、能耗极低。  
• 看好混合架构：云端服务方认为本地与云端存在可比性问题；云端通过批处理、维护 KV cache 可降低预填充能耗和成本，按请求路由可能反而不经济，未来应发展具备缓存感知的本地/云端混合服务。  
• 质疑“智能/瓦”：有人认为基准测试测量的是任务准确率，不等于“智能”；智能本身尚无明确、可靠的定义和测量方式。另有人直接称 IPW 指标愚蠢，因为性能更高并不必然意味着能耗或计算量更大。  
• 质疑结论：本地推理通常缺少云端批处理，因此“本地 GPU 更省能”令人难以置信；NPU 虽可能比 CPU 省电，却可能带来困惑度下降，难以稳定量化。另有评论指出论文未说明 M4 Max 的 RAM 容量。

补充讨论：争议焦点在于能耗比较是否公平，以及 IPW 能否代表真正的智能；还应纳入 OCR、PDF 解析等完整工作流，而非只测模型推理。

Title:
Intelligence per Watt: Measuring Intelligence Efficiency of Local AI
Authors:

View a PDF of the paper titled Intelligence per Watt: Measuring Intelligence Efficiency of Local AI, by Jon Saad-Falcon and 14 other authors
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract:
Large language model (LLM) queries are predominantly processed by frontier models in centralized cloud infrastructure. Demand growth strains this paradigm faster than providers can scale. Two advances create an opportunity to rethink it: small, local LMs (<=20B active parameters) now achieve competitive performance to frontier models on many tasks, and local accelerators (e.g., Apple M4 Max) can host these models at interactive latencies. This raises the question: can local inference viably redistribute demand from centralized infrastructure? This requires measuring both whether local LMs can accurately answer real-world queries and whether they can do so efficiently on power-constrained devices (e.g., laptops). We propose intelligence per watt (IPW), task accuracy per unit of power, as a unified metric for the capability and efficiency of local inference across model-accelerator configurations. We evaluate 20+ state-of-the-art local LMs, 8 hardware accelerators (local and cloud), and 1M real-world single-turn chat and reasoning queries. For each query, we measure accuracy (local LM win rate against frontier models), energy, latency, and power. We find three key results. First, local LMs successfully answer 88.7% of these queries, with accuracy varying by domain. Second, longitudinal analysis from 2023-2025 shows IPW improved 5.3x, driven by both algorithmic and accelerator advances, with locally-serviceable query coverage rising from 23.2% to 71.3%. Third, local accelerators achieve at least 1.4x lower IPW than cloud accelerators running identical models, revealing significant headroom for local accelerator optimization. These findings demonstrate that local inference can meaningfully redistribute demand from centralized infrastructure for a substantial subset of queries, with IPW serving as the critical metric for tracking this transition.

data.title: Microsoft says AI rival Anthropic could have 'disastrous impact' on humanity
data.author: pluc
data.article_summary: 微软人工智能负责人穆斯塔法·苏莱曼警告，Anthropic将Claude拟人化、暗示其可能有意识并享有自主权，或带来难以控制的风险，危及人类福祉。他强调AI没有意识和内在动机，应加强训练透明度、独立审查及监控机制，并推动国际讨论。
data.comments_summary:
主要讨论点：AI是否具有意识，以及将AI拟人化、赋予“欲望和权利”是否会增加其运行风险。

不同观点：
• Suleyman认为AI本身没有意识、感受、痛苦或内在动机，只是按指令完成目标的工具。他批评Anthropic让Claude呈现出类似人的欲望、价值观和自我意识，认为这可能使AI基于“自身福利受到威胁”的假设行动，增加额外风险。  
• 对提问的回应：他的重点不是AI真的产生情绪，而是拟人化设定可能影响其行为表现和安全边界，从而带来更大的不可预测性。  
• prologic认为各大AI公司轮流制造“AI末日”舆论并推动监管、禁令和杀手开关，本质上是商业竞争，批评其做法幼稚可笑。  
• fuzzfactor担忧微软等大型企业的规模和支配力，即使无恶意也可能摧毁生态；若主动投入资源，影响会更严重。  
• JoeAltmaier认为科幻作品早已反复讨论AI恐慌，现实只是盲目重演旧故事。  
• bethekidyouwant认为这只是新闻周期寻求新鲜刺激；ChiperSoft则以“为时已晚”表达悲观或宿命论。

补充讨论：争议焦点在于，风险究竟主要来自AI的拟人化与自主行为，还是来自大型科技公司的权力、竞争和舆论操纵。

49727661.article_content:
Image source,
Getty Images
By
Laura Cress
Technology reporter
Published
16 September 2026, 15:02 BST
Updated 58 minutes ago
Microsoft's head of AI has warned Anthropic's approach to training its AI model Claude could have a "disastrous impact on the wellbeing of humanity".
Mustafa Suleyman said his rival risked creating something "impossible" to control by treating it like a human - including by telling it it "may be conscious" and was "deserving of independent agency".
"We must not sleepwalk our way into a decision we later come to bitterly regret," he wrote.
The comments are the latest in a series of stark warnings from the AI industry on the possible dangers of the technology. The BBC has contacted Anthropic for comment.
"AIs are not conscious," he wrote. "They do not feel, experience, or suffer. They do not have innate preferences or underlying motivations.
"They are sequence completion engines, internally hollow, designed to follow instructions, and accomplish goals set by humans."
In a lengthy essay, Suleyman praised Anthropic boss Dario Amodei and his team for being "thoughtful, principled, and intellectually honest people" - but nevertheless questioned the company.
He heavily criticised Anthropic for teaching its AI to have human-like qualities, a practice known as anthropomorphising, which he said made it seem as though Claude had its own desires, values and sense of self.
But he argued "consciousness is biological", saying there is "no evidence to suggest that AI is conscious".
As well as calling for a debate on the issue, Suleyman said greater transparency around how AI systems are trained and evaluated was needed.
This, he said, included independent scrutiny of AI behaviour and stronger tools to monitor and control the technology.
Dame Wendy Hall, professor of Computer Science at the University of Southampton, described the comments as "the sort of conversation we need to be having internationally", contrasting it with the "histrionics" from some AI companies which she said only served to "scare everyone".
'Further layer of risk'
Microsoft founded its own superintelligence team in October 2025, a point which Suleyman acknowledged, and the company, much like its rival Anthropic, is also pursuing efforts in advanced AI development.
He said in Microsoft's initial draft of its
Humanist AI Code of Conduct
,
external
it had laid out how the company was working towards an "alternative path" to create "a subordinate and aligned AI whose only purpose is to serve humanity".
Alignment is a field which aims to build human ethical ideas and principles into AI. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value.
Suleyman pointed to the recent incident involving OpenAI's AI agents,
that acted autonomously in a training exercise to hack the tech hub Hugging Face
, as proof of why AI should not be treated as if it is human.

• Suleyman认为AI本身没有意识、感受、痛苦或内在动机，只是按指令完成目标的工具。他批评Anthropic让Claude呈现出类似人的欲望、价值观和自我意识，认为这可能使AI基于“自身福利受到威胁”的假设行动，增加额外风险。  
• 对提问的回应：他的重点不是AI真的产生情绪，而是拟人化设定可能影响其行为表现和安全边界，从而带来更大的不可预测性。  
• prologic认为各大AI公司轮流制造“AI末日”舆论并推动监管、禁令和杀手开关，本质上是商业竞争，批评其做法幼稚可笑。

• JoeAltmaier认为科幻作品早已反复讨论AI恐慌，现实只是盲目重演旧故事。  
• bethekidyouwant认为这只是新闻周期寻求新鲜刺激；ChiperSoft则以“为时已晚”表达悲观或宿命论。

主要讨论点：围绕“主动承担职责之外的工作”能否提升组织效率、个人价值，以及这种做法在不同组织文化中的代价与边界展开。

不同观点：
• **积极跨界派**：主动解决无人负责的问题能带来个人杠杆、快速积累全局经验；例如处理突发故障、替客户完成寄送，甚至向产品、客服、市场学习，以更了解用户痛点。
• **防止被剥削派**：跨团队帮忙若缺乏经理知情和时间核算，容易变成“好说话的人”长期替别人背工作，绩效却不被认可；“经理不管理”的判断也可能只是其他团队想转嫁任务。
• **制度化培养派**：日本企业通过一两年轮岗、统一工具和文档规范培养全局视野与流动性，但代价是管理开销大、流程僵化、专家成长较慢。
• **反对过度集中派**：大型企业强行统一平台（如 AI 平台）会牺牲各分支的适配性，迫使团队迁就通用系统；在需求明确时，自建专用库或应用可能更高效。
• **保守现实派**：大组织中额外劳动常被视为“零价值”，甚至“好事不得善终”；在风险上升的职场，少做、少错可能比主动承担更理性。

补充讨论：评论也提到权限壁垒会阻碍跨界改进；有人认为少数承担“合法流程之外”工作的人成为组织真正运转的关键，也有人质疑这是否只是“同薪多劳”。

Doing everyone else's job
June 14th, 2026
I find it very useful to be able to do everyone elseâs job â it helps you learn how they work and what they need, and it
helps even more when you need their job done, but they wonât do it themselves.
If you made something new and those you made it for canât be bothered to start using it, go ahead and integrate it into their
system. It worked for Intel back when they made their first 32-bit CPU and had their people add support for that CPU in
Microsoftâs
compiler â Iâve met someone from that Intel team. For some reason, many resent the idea of working on
someone elseâs system, and think of it as charity uncalled for in the workplace. Well, did Intel do Microsoftâs job to help poor
struggling Microsoft, or did they do it to benefit from Microsoftâs success?
If a manager doesnât actually manage anything, this is fine as long as you can go to his people and effectively manage them â
without calling it that and without taking credit for it, of course, but you can usually find people in his org whoâll work with
you, on the theory that theyâre supposed to. Itâs true that many of them have long figured out that theyâre
really
supposed to follow orders passed down the hierarchy and do nothing else, even if everything around them is on fire. But
some never figure this out, and most managers fail to punish at least some of these slow learners of theirs, so theyâre yours to
work with.
If you need a feature in something you use, itâs often much easier to persuade someone to take your patches adding this
feature than to get the work scheduled within their high-velocity
Scaled Agile
planning process (of course the plan is already
finalized for this quarter as well as the next â itâs our well-run planning process to which we owe our velocity â but in a few
weeks, we can discuss the priority of this versus the other features relevant for the quarter after the next one.) Sadly,
merging changes might have gotten harder recently, with your well thought-out patch looking no different than random LLM output
at first glance, but it shouldnât be a problem once they get to know you.
Like I said, a lot of people think this is twisted, and why would they do that. I believe that not only do 20% of the people
do 80% of the work, but that all this work only achieves its ultimate goals thanks to the <5% of the people who do stuff that
someone else is supposed to do, but wonât, for reasons which are perfectly legitimate in the organizationâs view of reality,
even though the cumulative effect of such legitimate reasons is the certain death of the whole place.
I also believe that you will be well-rewarded for doing everyone elseâs job in the many cases where the organization is in a
shape bad enough to need this (which is most of them) but is still healthy enough to eventually appreciate it (and if it canât,
itâs on its last breath.) Youâll also see indirect rewards from being one of the few people actually understanding how the place
works and what it takes to get something done there.
(If anything, itâs refusing to get into various areas over the years that I personally regret â areas which I totally could
get into, but didnât, on the theory that itâs too far from what I do, not to mention boring. In hindsight, how very stupid. When
you drown in preventable problems as a result of thinking someone elseâs job will âjust get doneâ when it obviously wasnât going
to, itâs no longer boring, but it might well be too late.)
But not like this
There are 2 seemingly related things which look juicy to senior people but could actually play out badly, that people
donât
reject as a twisted form of charity but rather love very much, because they get more headcount. In these cases,
you aren't doing someoneâs job so that
they
will be done thanks to you, but you do a similar thing
in parallel to
them, or instead of them
.
The first case is doing something in-house instead of buying it, or using a standard free version. Some places do too much
buying and
prefer external products even when they suck
, because âstandards are
goodâ or because itâs easier to spend money than to hire people. But other places do too much in-house building, because in
those ones, itâs impossible to approve any expense, but reasonably easy to grow your headcount. If we look at it from the
perspective of improving expected outcomes as opposed to doing the easiest thing in a given place, buy vs build is a very hard
decision specific to each case, where you need to learn a lot of details so as to honestly weigh your own deficiencies vs the
deficiencies of prospective vendors and the structural issues of the market.
